## Core idea

Do not stop at the first idea. Generate alternatives, compare them with the need, then communicate the strongest concept clearly enough for someone else to understand and question it.

## Generate alternatives

Use quick sketches, shape combinations, material changes, alternate orientations, and “borrow–combine–adapt–improve” prompts. At this stage, quantity creates options; evaluation comes next.

For each alternative, identify:

- the requirement it addresses;
- the restriction it respects;
- what makes it meaningfully different;
- one uncertainty that needs a test.

## Communicate the concept

A useful concept package may include:

- a short statement connecting the situation, need, and proposed response;
- a labelled sketch or digital drawing;
- critical dimensions and materials;
- a user flow, exploded view, sequence, or interface state where appropriate;
- the decision criteria used to select the concept;
- a specific question for feedback.

Communication is not decoration. It is a test of whether the idea is coherent and whether other people can identify gaps before time and material are spent.

## Feedback that changes the work

Ask users and peers what they understand, what seems missing, and what could fail. Record patterns instead of defending the first version. Decide what to keep, change, test, or defer.

Use the [N.I.C.E. Communicate, Feedback, and Plan resources](../../teaching-materials/nice-design-process/index.qmd) for printable and online classroom formats.
